image-compressor.intro: The Image Compressor reduces the file size of JPG, PNG, and WebP images without changing their pixel dimensions. It re-encodes each image in your browser using the Canvas API, so files never leave your device unless you explicitly save them to the cloud. A quality slider balances visual fidelity against file size with a live estimate, batch processing handles up to 20 images at once, and results download individually or as a single ZIP archive.

knowledge.heading: How lossy compression discards detail
knowledge.body: JPG and WebP are lossy formats: they shrink files by discarding high-frequency visual detail that the human eye notices least. The quality slider controls how aggressively this detail is dropped — lower values produce smaller files but introduce blocky artifacts, especially in smooth gradients and text. PNG is lossless, so the slider has no effect on PNG output, which always preserves every pixel. For screenshots or images with sharp text, prefer PNG or a high JPG quality to keep edges crisp.

faq.q: What quality should I use for web images?
faq.a: For most photographs destined for the web, a JPG quality between 70 and 80 is a good starting point — it typically halves the file size with little perceptible loss. Increase to 85 to 90 for hero images where detail matters, or drop to 60 for thumbnails and previews where small size is the priority.

faq.q: Does compressing multiple times degrade quality?
faq.a: Yes. Every lossy re-encode of JPG or WebP discards a little more detail, a phenomenon called generation loss. To avoid compounding artifacts, compress from the original source file each time rather than re-compressing an already-compressed copy.

image-resizer.intro: The Image Resizer changes the pixel dimensions of JPG, PNG, and WebP images. Choose exact pixels, a percentage scale, or a common preset, and lock the aspect ratio for a contain fit that avoids stretching. Batch processing resizes a whole folder to one specification at once. All work happens locally in your browser, with no upload and no server-side processing.

knowledge.heading: Resolution, pixel dimensions, and print size
knowledge.body: An image's pixel dimensions (width by height) define how many pixels it contains, while resolution (PPI or DPI) describes how densely those pixels are printed on paper. Resizing changes the pixel count, not the resolution metadata. A 2000 by 1000 image printed at 100 PPI covers 20 by 10 inches; the same file at 300 PPI covers roughly 6.7 by 3.3 inches. For screen use, only the pixel dimensions matter — set them to match your layout and let the browser handle the rest.

faq.q: What is the difference between resize and crop?
faq.a: Resizing scales the entire image uniformly — every pixel stays, just larger or smaller. Cropping removes part of the image to change its framing or aspect ratio. Use resize when you need smaller dimensions; use the Image Cropper when you need a different composition or a fixed aspect ratio.

faq.q: Should I resize before or after compressing?
faq.a: Resize first, then compress. Smaller dimensions mean fewer pixels to encode, which compounds the file-size savings from compression. Resizing after heavy compression will not recover detail already lost, so establishing the target dimensions up front gives the best quality-to-size ratio.

image-converter.intro: The Image Converter transforms images between JPG, PNG, and WebP. Because JPG has no transparency, converting a PNG or WebP with transparent areas to JPG fills those pixels with a background color you choose. The output file extension always matches the real encoded MIME type, so a JPG-encoded file never ships with a misleading name. Batch conversion handles multiple files at once, with results downloadable individually or as a ZIP.

knowledge.heading: When to choose WebP over JPG or PNG
knowledge.body: WebP supports both lossy and lossless compression plus transparency in a single format, and typically produces smaller files than equivalent JPGs or PNGs. Modern browsers support it universally, making it a strong default for web assets. Use JPG when you need maximum compatibility with older systems, and PNG when you need guaranteed lossless output with sharp text or logos. WebP is the best all-round choice for the web today.

faq.q: Why does my transparent PNG get a white background as JPG?
faq.a: JPG does not support an alpha channel, so transparent pixels must be filled with a solid color during conversion — white by default. Pick a background color that matches where the image will be placed, or convert to WebP or PNG instead if you need to keep transparency.

faq.q: Is converting PNG to JPG lossy?
faq.a: Yes. PNG is lossless and JPG is lossy, so the conversion re-encodes the image and may introduce artifacts, particularly in areas of sharp contrast. If quality is critical, keep the PNG or convert to WebP with a high quality setting.

image-cropper.intro: The Image Cropper trims JPG, PNG, and WebP images to a free region or a fixed aspect ratio such as 1:1, 4:3, 3:2, or 16:9. A 90-degree rotation toggle reorients the image before cropping, and the editor works with both mouse and touch on mobile. Cropping runs entirely in your browser — no upload, no server round-trip.

knowledge.heading: Aspect ratios for common platforms
knowledge.body: Different platforms favor different aspect ratios: Instagram square posts use 1:1 and landscape posts 1.91:1; YouTube thumbnails 16:9; many social share images 16:9; cover photos vary by network. Cropping to the target ratio before upload avoids automatic platform cropping that may cut off the wrong part of your image. Lock the ratio, position the crop, and export at the platform's recommended resolution for best results.

faq.q: Can I crop to a custom aspect ratio?
faq.a: Yes. Choose the free crop mode to drag an unconstrained region, or enter a custom ratio if your use case needs a specific proportion. The fixed presets (1:1, 4:3, 3:2, 16:9) are there for convenience and cover most common output shapes.

faq.q: Does cropping reduce file size?
faq.a: Usually yes — removing pixels reduces the data the encoder must store, so the output file is often smaller than the source. The reduction depends on how much of the image you cut away; combine cropping with the Image Compressor for the smallest possible output.

compress-image-to-kb.intro: Compress Image to KB shrinks a JPG, PNG, or WebP image to a target file size you specify — 50 KB, 100 KB, 200 KB, or any value. It runs a bounded quality search that finds the highest quality setting meeting your target, and reports honestly when a target is not reachable (for example, a very detailed image that cannot fit in 20 KB without severe artifacts). Processing is local; nothing is uploaded.

knowledge.heading: Why some targets are unreachable
knowledge.body: Lossy compression can only discard so much detail before an image becomes unusable. A small target applied to a large, detailed source forces very low quality settings, and if even quality zero exceeds the target, the goal is mathematically impossible without reducing pixel dimensions. The tool tells you when this happens instead of silently producing a broken file — combine it with the Image Resizer to first reduce dimensions, then target the size.

faq.q: How is this different from the regular compressor?
faq.a: The regular Image Compressor lets you pick a quality level and shows the resulting size. Compress to KB reverses that relationship: you state the size you need, and the tool searches for the highest quality that fits. Use it when a platform or email system enforces a hard size cap.

faq.q: What target should I pick for email attachments?
faq.a: Most email providers cap attachments around 25 MB total, but individual images of 200 to 500 KB display well and leave room for the message. For inline thumbnails, 50 to 100 KB is usually plenty. Pick the smallest target that still looks acceptable to keep your message light.

rotate-image.intro: Rotate Image turns JPG, PNG, and WebP images by 90, 180, or 270 degrees, and mirrors them horizontally or vertically (flip). Batch processing applies the same rotation to many files at once. Because 90-degree steps swap width and height, the canvas is resized to match — no content is lost. All processing happens locally in your browser.

knowledge.heading: Lossless rotation and EXIF orientation
knowledge.body: Rotating an image by 90-degree steps is mathematically lossless when the format supports it — pixels are rearranged, not re-encoded. However, photos taken on phones often carry an EXIF orientation tag that tells software how to display them; some viewers honor it and some do not, which is why a phone photo may appear sideways on a desktop. Re-encoding after rotation bakes the orientation into the actual pixels, so the image displays correctly everywhere even if the viewer ignores EXIF.

faq.q: Will rotation reduce image quality?
faq.a: For 90, 180, and 270 degree rotations of JPG images, the pixels are rearranged rather than re-sampled, so quality is preserved as much as the format allows. Other angles, which this tool does not offer, require resampling and can soften edges. Flipping is also lossless in the same way.

faq.q: Can I rotate multiple images by different angles?
faq.a: This version applies one rotation choice to the whole batch. If you need per-image angles, run the tool once per group of images that share the same rotation, or rotate them one at a time.

watermark-image.intro: Watermark Image stamps a text watermark onto JPG, PNG, and WebP images. Position it on a 9-point grid, set opacity and angle, or repeat it as a diagonal tile across the whole image to deter image theft. Batch processing watermarks many files with the same settings at once. Everything runs locally — your images are not uploaded.

knowledge.heading: Visible vs invisible watermarking
knowledge.body: A visible watermark is text or a logo overlaid on the image — what this tool produces — making ownership obvious and discouraging casual reuse. An invisible, steganographic watermark encodes ownership data into the pixels imperceptibly and requires special software to detect. Visible watermarks are the practical choice for protecting previews and portfolios: position a tiled, semi-transparent mark across the image so it cannot be easily cropped out.

faq.q: How do I make a watermark hard to remove?
faq.a: Use the tile (repeat) mode to cover the whole image with a diagonal pattern of marks at moderate opacity. A single corner watermark is trivially cropped out; a full tiled pattern forces a remover to reconstruct the underlying image, which is rarely worth the effort.

faq.q: What opacity should I use?
faq.a: For portfolio previews, 20 to 35 percent opacity is enough to assert ownership without obscuring the image. For proofing or stock samples where you want to discourage use entirely, 50 to 70 percent is common. Test on a few images and adjust before batch-processing the full set.

meme-generator.intro: The Meme Generator turns any JPG, PNG, or WebP image into a meme with classic bold top and bottom captions. The outlined lettering stays legible over any background, light or dark. Adjust font size and position to fit the image, then download the result. All rendering happens in your browser — no upload, no watermark added.

knowledge.heading: The classic meme caption style
knowledge.body: The recognizable meme caption uses a heavy, condensed sans-serif in white with a black outline, placed at the top and bottom of the image. The outline is created by drawing the text multiple times in black offset by a few pixels in each direction, then the white fill on top. This technique keeps text readable over any background without needing a solid banner behind it, which is why the style became the default for image macros.

faq.q: Can I add text in the middle of the image?
faq.a: This tool focuses on the classic top-and-bottom caption layout. For free-form text anywhere on the image — multiple blocks, arbitrary positions, stickers — use the Photo Editor, which lets you drag text and emoji onto the canvas with a live preview.

faq.q: What font does the meme generator use?
faq.a: It uses a bold, Impact-style condensed typeface rendered with a black outline, matching the classic image-macro look. If your browser lacks the exact font, a close system equivalent is used so the result keeps the same bold, outlined appearance.

photo-editor.intro: The Photo Editor adjusts brightness, contrast, and saturation, applies filters, and lets you drag text and emoji stickers onto your image with a live preview. All adjustments are non-destructive until you export, so you can experiment freely. The editor works with mouse and touch, and everything runs locally — your photo is never uploaded.

knowledge.heading: Non-destructive adjustment order
knowledge.body: Adjustments interact: brightness shifts all pixel values up or down, contrast stretches or compresses the range around a midpoint, and saturation scales color intensity. Applying brightness before contrast differs from the reverse order. This tool applies adjustments in a fixed pipeline and shows the combined result live, so what you see is what you export. For subtle results, make small moves and check the preview at full size before downloading.

faq.q: Are the filters destructive?
faq.a: Filters are preview-only until you export — you can toggle and combine them while editing, and the original image stays intact on disk. Once you download the result, the adjustments are baked into the exported file, so keep the original separately if you may want to re-edit later.

faq.q: Can I undo changes?
faq.a: Yes — toggle a filter off or reset a slider to its default to remove an adjustment before export. Because edits are live and non-destructive, you can freely experiment and only the final state is exported when you download.

blur-image.intro: Blur Image lets you draw rectangles over faces, license plates, or any sensitive area and blur or pixelate them. Everything runs locally in your browser — the image is never uploaded — so it is safe for privacy-sensitive material. Toggle between Gaussian blur and mosaic (pixelate) effects, and adjust the intensity to taste.

knowledge.heading: Blur vs pixelate for privacy
knowledge.body: Gaussian blur smooths detail into a soft gradient, which looks natural but can sometimes be reversed by sophisticated deblurring software on simple patterns. Pixelation (mosaic) replaces the region with larger blocks of average color, which destroys fine detail more aggressively and is harder to reconstruct. For maximum privacy on sensitive content like faces or plates, pixelation at a coarse block size is the safer choice; blur is fine for aesthetic effect or mild obfuscation.

faq.q: Can blur be reversed?
faq.a: Strong Gaussian blur on simple, regular patterns has been partially reversed in research settings using deconvolution. For genuinely sensitive content, use pixelation at a coarse block size, or cover the area completely with a solid fill. The risk is low for most everyday use, but not zero for determined attackers.

faq.q: How do I blur multiple faces at once?
faq.a: Draw a separate rectangle over each face — each region is blurred independently. You can mix blur and pixelate regions in the same image if some areas need stronger obfuscation than others. Adjust the intensity before exporting the final result.

steps: Drag your JPG, PNG, or WebP image into the drop zone, or click to pick files. You can add several at once.
Choose an output format — keep the original, or convert to JPG, PNG, or WebP.
Drag the quality slider. Lower quality means a smaller file; the live estimate updates as you move it.
Click Compress. Each image is processed in your browser and appears in the list with its new size and savings.
Download images one by one, or download all results as a ZIP. Sign-in users can also save an original or result to their private cloud.
useCases: Shrinking photos before attaching them to an email that has a size limit.
Reducing page weight on a blog or storefront so images load faster.
Batch-compressing a folder of product photos for an online store.
Trimming screenshots before pasting them into a document or chat.

knowledge.heading: JPG vs PNG vs WebP for compression
knowledge.body: JPG and WebP are lossy formats, so the quality slider controls how much detail is discarded and directly affects file size. PNG is lossless — the slider has no effect on PNG output, which is best when you need every pixel preserved, such as screenshots with sharp text.

knowledge.heading: Why compression happens in your browser
knowledge.body: Your image is decoded and re-encoded locally using the browser's Canvas and ImageBitmap APIs. The bytes never leave your device unless you explicitly choose to save a file to your cloud storage, so there is no upload to wait for and no copy on a server.

faq.q: Is there a file size limit?
faq.a: Yes — a single image can be up to 25 MB and roughly 40 megapixels, with up to 20 files per batch. These limits protect your browser's memory during decoding.

faq.q: Will compression reduce the resolution?
faq.a: No. The compressor changes encoding quality, not dimensions. Use the Image Resizer if you also need smaller pixel dimensions.

faq.q: Are my images uploaded?
faq.a: No. Processing is local-first. Files are only uploaded if you are signed in and click a Save to cloud button.

steps: Add one or more JPG, PNG, or WebP images to the drop zone.
Pick a mode: resize by exact pixels, by percentage, or using a common preset.
Enter the target width and/or height. With the aspect-ratio lock on, the other dimension updates automatically for a contain fit.
Click Resize. Each result shows the before-and-after dimensions.
Download individually or as a ZIP; signed-in users can save results to their private cloud.
useCases: Fitting a cover photo or banner to an exact platform dimension.
Scaling a batch of photos down for a slideshow or thumbnail grid.
Preparing images so a web page stays under a layout budget.
Shrinking phone photos before sharing over a slow connection.

knowledge.heading: Contain fit and aspect ratio
knowledge.body: Locking the aspect ratio gives you a contain fit: the image is scaled so it fits entirely within the target box without stretching or cropping. If you need an exact crop to a ratio instead, use the Image Cropper.

knowledge.heading: Upscaling is discouraged
knowledge.body: Scaling an image up does not add real detail — it just interpolates existing pixels, which looks soft. The tool allows it but flags unusually large outputs so you know the result may not be sharp.

faq.q: Can I resize to a percentage instead of pixels?
faq.a: Yes. Switch to percentage mode and enter a scale like 50%. The new pixel dimensions are computed from the original size.

faq.q: What happens to very large images?
faq.a: Images near the browser's memory limits are flagged. You can still process them, but reducing the batch size helps avoid slow decoding.

faq.q: Does resizing change the file format?
faq.a: Only if you choose a different output format. By default the original format is kept.

steps: Drop in JPG, PNG, or WebP images.
Choose the target format: JPG, PNG, or WebP.
If you are converting to JPG, pick a background color — JPG has no transparency, so transparent areas are filled with this color.
Click Convert. The list shows the before-and-after format and size, and the downloaded file always has the correct extension for its real type.
Download individually or as a ZIP; signed-in users can save results to cloud storage.
useCases: Converting a transparent PNG to JPG for a platform that does not accept PNG.
Turning a folder of JPGs into WebP for smaller web assets.
Changing screenshots to PNG to keep text crisp and lossless.
Normalizing mixed file types in a batch before uploading to a system that wants one format.

knowledge.heading: Transparency and the JPG format
knowledge.body: JPG does not support an alpha channel. When you convert a PNG or WebP with transparent pixels to JPG, those pixels are filled with the background color you choose — white by default — so logos and cut-outs land on a solid backdrop instead of black.

knowledge.heading: The extension always matches the real MIME type
knowledge.body: The output file extension is derived from the bytes that are actually produced, not the name you typed, so a JPG-encoded file never ships with a .png extension that would confuse browsers and CMSes.

faq.q: Does conversion reduce quality?
faq.a: Converting to JPG or WebP re-encodes the image and can introduce lossy artifacts. Converting to PNG is lossless. Use the Image Compressor if you want finer quality control.

faq.q: Can I convert HEIC or AVIF?
faq.a: Not in this version. HEIC and AVIF support depends on the browser and is planned once capability detection is reliable.

faq.q: Is batch conversion supported?
faq.a: Yes. Add multiple files and convert them all, then download as a ZIP.

steps: Choose an image to load into the cropper.
Pick a free crop or a fixed aspect ratio preset: 1:1, 4:3, 3:2, or 16:9.
Drag the crop rectangle with the mouse or your finger. Use the zoom control for precise placement.
Rotate in 90° steps if the source is sideways.
Click Crop & preview to see the result, then download. You can choose a different output format or start over with another image.
useCases: Cutting a profile picture to a 1:1 square.
Cropping a photo to 16:9 for a YouTube thumbnail or cover.
Trimming wasted space around a screenshot before sharing.
Fixing a sideways phone photo with a quick 90° rotation.

knowledge.heading: Aspect ratio presets
knowledge.body: A preset locks the crop to a fixed ratio so the output fits a known slot — 1:1 for avatars, 4:3 and 3:2 for classic photo prints, and 16:9 for widescreen covers. Free mode lets you crop to any shape.

knowledge.heading: Works with touch
knowledge.body: The crop rectangle supports pointer and touch events, so it works on phones and tablets as well as desktops. Pinch-to-zoom is handled by the zoom control.

faq.q: Can I rotate the image?
faq.a: Yes, in 90° steps. Use the rotation control before cropping if the photo was taken sideways.

faq.q: Does cropping upload my image?
faq.a: No. Cropping happens entirely in your browser.

faq.q: Can I crop multiple images at once?
faq.a: The cropper works on one image at a time so you can fine-tune each frame. Use the batch tools for bulk operations.

steps: Add a JPG, PNG, or WebP image.
Pick a target size — 50 KB, 100 KB, 200 KB, 500 KB, 1 MB — or enter a custom target in KB.
Optionally allow PNG to WebP conversion if you are willing to lose transparency to reach the target.
Click Compress to target. The tool runs a bounded quality search and tells you the result honestly.
Download the result. If the target could not be reached, the closest result is returned and noted under the file.
useCases: Hitting a strict upload limit on a form, marketplace, or government portal.
Preparing an avatar or badge that must be under a specific KB cap.
Compressing an email attachment to fit a provider's size rule.
Producing a thumbnail that meets a size budget for a CMS.

knowledge.heading: A bounded search, not a guess
knowledge.body: The tool searches quality values in a bounded range with an iteration and time limit — never an infinite loop. It measures each candidate's real encoded size and stops at the best fit, so the reported size is the actual output size.

knowledge.heading: Not every target is reachable
knowledge.body: A tiny, detailed photo cannot always be compressed to an aggressive KB target without unacceptable quality loss. When that happens the tool returns the closest result and says so plainly, instead of silently degrading the image.

faq.q: What if the target size cannot be reached?
faq.a: The closest achievable result is returned and a note under the file explains that the target was not met, so you can decide whether to accept it or try a larger target.

faq.q: Why might PNG → WebP be offered?
faq.a: PNG is lossless and often large. If you allow it, converting to WebP can reach a KB target that PNG cannot, at the cost of transparency and some quality.

faq.q: Is there an iteration limit?
faq.a: Yes. The search has a maximum number of iterations and a time budget, so it always terminates.

steps: Add one or more images to the drop zone.
Pick a rotation: 0°, 90°, 180°, or 270°.
Optionally flip horizontally or vertically (or both).
Click Rotate. A live preview shows the effect on the first image before you process the batch.
Download individually or as a ZIP; signed-in users can save results to cloud storage.
useCases: Fixing phone photos that imported sideways.
Mirroring an image for a design or print layout.
Rotating a batch of scanned pages to the same orientation.
Creating a flipped version of a logo or graphic.

knowledge.heading: 90° steps keep quality intact
knowledge.body: Rotating by 90°, 180°, or 270° rearranges pixels without re-sampling, so there is no quality loss from the rotation itself. The only re-encoding happens when you choose an output format.

knowledge.heading: Flip vs rotate
knowledge.body: Flipping mirrors the image along an axis — like a reflection — while rotating turns it around its center. You can combine a flip with a rotation in a single pass.

faq.q: Can I rotate by an arbitrary angle like 15°?
faq.a: This tool rotates in 90° steps to avoid re-sampling artifacts. For free-angle rotation, use the Photo Editor's transform options.

faq.q: Does rotating reduce quality?
faq.a: No. 90°-step rotation and flips preserve all pixels; only the chosen output format affects quality.

faq.q: Can I process multiple images?
faq.a: Yes. Add several files and rotate them all with the same settings.

steps: Add one or more images.
Type your watermark text.
Choose a position on the 9-point grid, or enable Repeat to tile the watermark diagonally across the whole image.
Adjust font size, color, opacity, and angle.
Click Watermark. A live preview shows the result on the first image; then download individually or as a ZIP.
useCases: Stamping a logo or name on portfolio photos before publishing.
Protecting preview images shared with clients.
Adding a repeating diagonal watermark to deter reuse of full-resolution exports.
Batch-watermarking product photos with a store name.

knowledge.heading: Single position vs repeat tile
knowledge.body: A single-position watermark sits in one of nine spots (corners, edges, or center). Repeat lays the text in an offset diagonal grid across the entire image, which is harder to crop out but more visually intrusive.

knowledge.heading: Opacity and angle
knowledge.body: Lower opacity makes a watermark less obtrusive but easier to remove visually. A slight angle (for example -20°) on a repeated tile reads as a classic diagonal stamp.

faq.q: Can I use an image or logo as the watermark?
faq.a: This tool applies a text watermark. For image-based overlays, use the Photo Editor's sticker and text layers.

faq.q: Does watermarking reduce image quality?
faq.a: It re-encodes the image once with your chosen output format. The watermark itself is drawn at full resolution.

faq.q: Can I watermark many images at once?
faq.a: Yes. Add a batch and the same watermark settings are applied to every file.

steps: Add an image to the drop zone.
Type the top text and/or bottom text.
Adjust the font size, text color, and outline color.
Click Generate meme. A live preview shows the result on the first image.
Download the meme; signed-in users can save it to cloud storage.
useCases: Turning a reaction photo into a shareable meme.
Adding a punchline caption to a screenshot for a chat or post.
Making quick top/bottom captions for a social draft.
Batch-captioning a set of template images with the same text.

knowledge.heading: Classic top and bottom text
knowledge.body: The generator uses the classic meme layout: uppercase text pinned to the top and bottom, drawn in a heavy Impact-style face with a contrasting outline so it stays readable over any background.

knowledge.heading: Text wraps to fit
knowledge.body: Long captions are word-wrapped to fit the image width, and bottom text is anchored from the bottom edge upward so it always sits at the base of the frame.

faq.q: Can I place text in the middle instead?
faq.a: This tool is focused on the classic top/bottom layout. For freely positioned text, use the Photo Editor and drag text layers anywhere.

faq.q: What format is the output?
faq.a: You can keep the original format or export as JPG, PNG, or WebP.

faq.q: Is there a live preview?
faq.a: Yes. As you type, the first image is re-rendered so you can see the caption before generating the batch.

steps: Load an image into the editor.
Adjust brightness, contrast, and saturation with the sliders, and pick a filter such as grayscale, sepia, invert, or vintage.
Add text layers and emoji stickers, then drag them into place on the live preview.
Select a layer to edit its text, size, or color, or delete it.
Click Export to download the edited image at full resolution. Reset clears all changes.
useCases: Quickly brightening and color-correcting a photo before posting.
Applying a vintage or sepia look to a set of images.
Adding a caption or emoji sticker to a picture for social media.
Light retouching without opening a heavy editor.

knowledge.heading: What you see is what you export
knowledge.body: The preview canvas mirrors the export: text and sticker sizes are stored as a fraction of the image height, so a caption that looks right in the preview renders at the same proportion in the full-resolution output.

knowledge.heading: Filters vs adjustments
knowledge.body: Brightness, contrast, and saturation are continuous adjustments applied through the canvas filter pipeline. Filter presets (grayscale, sepia, invert, vintage) stack on top for a one-click look.

faq.q: Can I add my own sticker image?
faq.a: Stickers are an emoji palette, which keeps the tool lightweight and asset-free. Text layers support any text and color.

faq.q: Does editing upload my photo?
faq.a: No. Everything runs in your browser. Export downloads the result directly.

faq.q: Can I edit multiple images?
faq.a: The editor works on one image at a time so the live preview stays responsive. Use the batch tools for bulk operations.

steps: Load an image into the blur tool.
Choose a mode: mosaic (pixelate) or gaussian blur.
Set the blur radius or mosaic tile size.
Drag on the image to draw a rectangle over the area you want to hide — faces, plates, text, or signatures. Add as many regions as you need.
Click Export to download the result. Clear regions removes all selections.
useCases: Blurring faces in photos before sharing them publicly.
Pixelating license plates, IDs, or addresses in screenshots.
Hiding sensitive text or signatures in a document scan.
Redacting parts of an image for a tutorial or bug report.

knowledge.heading: Mosaic vs gaussian blur
knowledge.body: Mosaic pixelates a region into blocky tiles, which is unmistakably redacted and hard to reverse. Gaussian blur softens the area smoothly, which looks more natural but is weaker for sensitive text. Use mosaic when you need to be sure the detail is gone.

knowledge.heading: Regions are drawn by you
knowledge.body: There is no automatic detection: you draw each rectangle, so you keep full control over exactly what is hidden and nothing is blurred by accident.

faq.q: Does the tool detect faces automatically?
faq.a: No. You draw each region yourself, which keeps the tool fully local and avoids any cloud-based detection. It also means you decide precisely what is obscured.

faq.q: Can I blur several areas?
faq.a: Yes. Draw as many rectangles as you need; each is applied to the export. Clear regions removes them all.

faq.q: Is the blur applied to the downloaded file?
faq.a: Yes. The export re-renders the image at full resolution with all your regions blurred or pixelated.

steps: Load a photo into the EXIF Viewer.
The tool reads the metadata locally in your browser — no upload.
Review the Image, Camera, and Settings groups for dimensions, orientation, make, lens, focal length, aperture, exposure, and ISO.
If the photo carries GPS data, see the coordinates and open them on a map.
Toggle “Show all fields” to inspect every raw EXIF value.
useCases: Checking what metadata a photo exposes before you share it publicly.
Verifying the camera settings used for a shot (focal length, aperture, ISO, exposure).
Finding the GPS location where a photo was taken.
Confirming whether orientation or software edits are embedded in the file.

knowledge.heading: What is EXIF metadata?
knowledge.body: EXIF (Exchangeable Image File Format) data is written by most cameras and phones into JPEG and TIFF files. It records the camera make and model, lens, exposure settings (aperture, shutter speed, ISO), focal length, date taken, orientation, and optionally GPS coordinates. Viewing it helps you understand how a photo was taken and what information it leaks.

knowledge.heading: Privacy and EXIF
knowledge.body: Photos taken on a phone often embed GPS coordinates, which can reveal your home or workplace. This viewer parses metadata locally so nothing is uploaded, but the same data is visible to anyone who receives the original file. Use the EXIF Remover tool before sharing sensitive photos.

faq.q: Does the EXIF Viewer upload my photo?
faq.a: No. The image is parsed entirely in your browser with a local library. The file never leaves your device.

faq.q: Why does my photo show no EXIF data?
faq.a: Some images have no EXIF — for example, PNG and WebP files rarely carry it, and images exported through certain editors or social platforms have metadata stripped. The viewer shows whatever is present.

faq.q: Can I remove EXIF after viewing it?
faq.a: Yes. Use the EXIF Remover tool to re-encode the image without metadata, then verify with this viewer that the fields are gone.

steps: Load a photo into the EXIF Remover.
The tool shows how many metadata fields are present and whether GPS is included.
Click Remove metadata. The image is re-encoded locally — no upload.
The output is re-parsed to verify that all EXIF, IPTC, XMP and GPS data is gone.
Download the clean image.
useCases: Stripping GPS coordinates before sharing a photo publicly.
Removing camera and lens details before uploading to a website.
Sharing a photo without revealing the date, location, or device it was taken with.
Preparing images for a clean public archive or stock library.

knowledge.heading: How re-encoding removes metadata
knowledge.body: When an image is decoded into a canvas and re-encoded, only the pixel data is kept — EXIF, IPTC, XMP, ICC and GPS blocks are not preserved by the canvas. This tool re-encodes the image locally and then parses the output bytes again to confirm zero metadata remains, rather than assuming the removal worked.

knowledge.heading: GPS and privacy
knowledge.body: Phones often tag photos with GPS coordinates that can pinpoint your home or workplace. Stripping metadata before sharing removes that leak. Some platforms also strip metadata on upload, but you cannot rely on every recipient doing so.

faq.q: Does removing EXIF reduce image quality?
faq.a: For PNG the re-encode is lossless, so there is no quality loss. For JPEG and WebP the image is re-encoded at high quality (0.92), which is visually near-identical to the original in almost all cases.

faq.q: How do I know the metadata is really gone?
faq.a: After removal, the tool parses the output file again and shows the remaining field count (zero) and confirms GPS is gone. You can also load the downloaded file into the EXIF Viewer to double-check.

faq.q: Does the EXIF Remover upload my photo?
faq.a: No. The image is decoded and re-encoded entirely in your browser. The file never leaves your device.

steps: Load a JPEG or PNG into the DPI Changer.
The tool reads the current DPI (if any) and shows the pixel dimensions.
Pick a preset (72, 96, 300, 600) or enter a custom DPI. A print-size preview updates live.
Click Apply DPI. The metadata is edited in place — pixels and EXIF are preserved, nothing is uploaded.
Download the image with the new DPI.
useCases: Setting a photo to 300 DPI for print submission.
Switching a screenshot to 72 DPI for web display.
Preparing a JPEG for a print shop that requires a specific DPI.
Checking the print size of an image at a given DPI before printing.

knowledge.heading: DPI metadata vs pixel resolution
knowledge.body: DPI (dots per inch) is metadata that tells software the intended physical size of an image when printed — it does not change the pixel data. A 3000px image at 300 DPI prints at 10 inches; at 72 DPI it prints at roughly 41.7 inches. The pixels are identical; only the printed size differs. Changing DPI never adds detail that was not already captured.

knowledge.heading: Why this tool is lossless
knowledge.body: The DPI Changer edits the resolution metadata in place — the JFIF density block for JPEG and the pHYs chunk for PNG — without re-encoding the pixel data. Your EXIF metadata (camera, lens, GPS) and image quality are preserved. Re-encoding through a canvas would strip metadata and re-compress; this tool avoids both.

faq.q: Does changing DPI make my image sharper?
faq.a: No. DPI is only metadata — it tells print software how large to print the image. It does not add pixels or increase detail. A low-resolution image stays low-resolution no matter what DPI you set.

faq.q: Why is WebP not supported?
faq.a: WebP stores resolution inside a RIFF/EXIF chunk that is more complex to edit losslessly. JPEG and PNG cover the vast majority of print-prep workflows; use the converter first if you have a WebP file.

faq.q: Is my EXIF metadata preserved?
faq.a: Yes. The tool edits only the DPI metadata (JFIF density for JPEG, pHYs for PNG) and leaves the rest of the file — including EXIF — untouched. Use the EXIF Remover if you want to strip metadata.

steps: Load a square image (a logo works best) into the Favicon Generator.
The tool generates PNGs at 16, 32, 48, 96, 180, 192 and 512px and a multi-size ICO (16/32/48).
Preview how the favicon looks at several sizes.
Copy the HTML snippet and download the ZIP — everything is generated locally, nothing is uploaded.
Place the files at your site root and paste the snippet into your <head>.
useCases: Creating a favicon set for a new website.
Generating an Apple touch icon and Android PWA icons from one logo.
Producing a multi-size ICO for legacy browser support.
Getting a ready-to-paste HTML snippet with all the link tags.

knowledge.heading: What goes in a favicon package
knowledge.body: A modern favicon set includes a multi-size ICO (favicon.ico) for legacy browsers, PNGs at 16/32px for browser tabs, a 180px apple-touch-icon.png for iOS home screens, and 192/512px PNGs plus a web manifest for Android/PWA install. This generator produces all of them from a single source image.

knowledge.heading: Square, simple images work best
knowledge.body: Favicons are tiny — 16px is the most common size — so detailed photos become muddy. Use a simple logo or mark, ideally square, with strong contrast. The source can be any size; it is scaled down to each target with the browser's default smoothing.

faq.q: Do I still need a .ico file?
faq.a: Most modern browsers accept PNG favicons, but a multi-size .ico (16/32/48) guarantees compatibility with older browsers and bookmarks. The package includes both, so you are covered everywhere.

faq.q: Where do I put the files?
faq.a: Place favicon.ico, the PNGs, and site.webmanifest at your site root, then paste the HTML snippet into the <head> of your pages. The paths in the snippet and manifest assume the site root.

faq.q: Can I use any image as the source?
faq.a: Yes — JPG, PNG or WebP. A square image with a simple logo produces the clearest favicons. Detailed photos work but lose detail at 16px.

steps: Load one or more JPG or PNG images into the tool.
Reorder the pages with the up and down buttons.
Choose a page size (A4 or Letter), orientation (auto, portrait, landscape), and margin.
Click Generate PDF — the file is built locally with pdf-lib, nothing is uploaded.
Download the single PDF with one image per page.
useCases: Combining scanned document pages into one PDF.
Building a PDF portfolio from a set of photos.
Creating a printable PDF from screenshots.
Sending several images as a single file.

knowledge.heading: One image per page, fit to the page
knowledge.body: Each image becomes one PDF page. The image is contain-fit into the page size minus the margins, preserving its aspect ratio — so it is never stretched or cropped. Auto orientation picks portrait or landscape per page based on each image's shape.

knowledge.heading: Why JPG and PNG only
knowledge.body: PDF embeds image data as-is, and pdf-lib supports embedding JPG and PNG directly. Other formats (WebP, GIF) are not part of the PDF image model; convert them to PNG or JPG first with the Image Converter.

faq.q: Does the tool compress my images when making the PDF?
faq.a: No. Images are embedded in the PDF at their original quality — pdf-lib inserts the JPG or PNG bytes directly. The PDF is roughly the sum of the input image sizes.

faq.q: Can I change the order of pages?
faq.a: Yes. Use the up and down buttons next to each image to reorder before generating. The PDF is built in the order shown.

faq.q: Is my data uploaded?
faq.a: No. The PDF is generated entirely in your browser with pdf-lib. The images never leave your device.

steps: Load a PDF file into the tool.
The tool reports the page count. Enter a page range like 1-3,5 or leave blank for all.
Choose a DPI (72, 150, or 300) and an output format (PNG or JPG).
Click Convert — each page is rendered locally with pdf.js, nothing is uploaded.
Download individual images or the whole set as a ZIP.
useCases: Extracting pages from a PDF as images for a presentation.
Converting a scanned PDF into image files.
Saving a single PDF page as a PNG for sharing.
Rasterizing a PDF for use in a tool that needs images.

knowledge.heading: DPI and render size
knowledge.body: PDFs are vector and have no fixed pixel size; the DPI you choose sets the render scale. 72 DPI matches the PDF's native point size (compact), 150 DPI is good for screen reading, and 300 DPI produces sharp, print-quality output. Higher DPI means larger image files.

knowledge.heading: Local rendering with pdf.js
knowledge.body: Rendering happens entirely in your browser with pdf.js (Mozilla's PDF engine). The PDF bytes never leave your device, and the pdf.js worker is served locally rather than from a CDN — consistent with the project's Local First principle.

faq.q: Why are my converted images large?
faq.a: Image size scales with DPI and page count. 300 DPI produces detailed but large images. Drop to 150 or 72 DPI for smaller files, or convert fewer pages.

faq.q: Can I convert only some pages?
faq.a: Yes. Enter a page range like 1-3,5 in the Page range field. Leave it blank to convert every page. Ranges are clamped to the document's page count.

faq.q: Is my PDF uploaded?
faq.a: No. The PDF is rendered entirely in your browser with pdf.js. The file never leaves your device.

steps: Drop or select multiple JPG, PNG, or WebP images.
Add one or more processing steps — resize, convert, compress, watermark, rotate, or rename — and reorder them.
Choose a concurrency level and click Process all.
Each file runs through the step pipeline locally; one failure never stops the batch.
Download individual results or the whole set as a ZIP.
useCases: Resizing a folder of photos for a website in one pass.
Converting a batch of PNGs to WebP.
Watermarking many images with the same text.
Renaming and compressing a set of exports at once.

knowledge.heading: A real pipeline, not a single op
knowledge.body: Each file flows through every step you add, in order — resize then compress then watermark, for example. Between steps the intermediate result is re-decoded so the next step sees the previous step's output. Steps reuse the same processing functions as the single tools, so results are identical.

knowledge.heading: Concurrency and isolation
knowledge.body: Files process with a small concurrency limit (1–3) to avoid exhausting browser memory. A failure on one file is isolated — it is marked failed and the rest continue. You can cancel pending work at any time; running tasks are interrupted best-effort.

faq.q: Is there a file or step limit?
faq.a: Each file must be under 25 MB and a supported image type (JPG, PNG, WebP). There is no hard step limit, but very long pipelines re-decode between steps, so they take longer per file.

faq.q: Does the batch upload my images?
faq.a: No. All processing happens in your browser. Images never leave your device, and results are only saved to the cloud if you explicitly choose to.

faq.q: What happens if one image fails?
faq.a: It is marked failed with the reason; every other file continues processing. You can fix the issue and re-run, or download the successful results.

steps: Load a JPG, PNG, or WebP image.
Pick a platform and a preset (e.g. Instagram Post, YouTube Thumbnail), or enter a custom width and height.
Choose a fit mode: Cover crops to fill the target, Contain fits inside with letterboxing.
Choose an output format (JPG, PNG, WebP).
Click Resize — the image is rendered locally, nothing is uploaded — then download the result.
useCases: Preparing an Instagram feed post or story.
Making a YouTube video thumbnail.
Sizing a Facebook page cover.
Creating a LinkedIn banner at the recommended ratio.

knowledge.heading: Cover vs Contain
knowledge.body: Cover scales the image to fill the entire target box and crops the overflow — best when the subject is centered and you want no empty space. Contain fits the whole image inside the box, leaving letterboxed bars — best when you must show the entire image.

knowledge.heading: Presets are recommendations, not rules
knowledge.body: The preset sizes are commonly recommended values, reviewed and dated. Platforms change their guidance and display sizes differently across devices. Treat these as starting points, not official enforced specifications — verify against the platform's current docs for production work.

faq.q: Are these the official platform sizes?
faq.a: They are commonly recommended sizes, each with a review date. Platforms update their guidance and display images differently across devices, so they are starting points rather than enforced rules.

faq.q: Can I use a custom size?
faq.a: Yes. Enter any width and height in the custom fields; they override the preset. The fit mode still applies to your custom target.

faq.q: Is my image uploaded?
faq.a: No. The resize runs entirely in your browser. The image never leaves your device.

steps: Load a JPG, PNG, or WebP image.
Optionally set a resize width and adjust the WebP quality.
Click Optimize — the image is converted to WebP and compressed locally, nothing is uploaded.
See the original size, result size, and percentage saved.
Download the optimized WebP.
useCases: Preparing hero images for a fast-loading website.
Converting photos to WebP for blog posts.
Shrinking large exports before uploading to a CMS.
Reducing bandwidth on image-heavy landing pages.

knowledge.heading: Why WebP for the web
knowledge.body: WebP delivers meaningfully smaller files than JPG and PNG at similar visual quality, and is now supported by all major browsers. Serving WebP can measurably improve page load time and Core Web Vitals.

knowledge.heading: Quality vs size
knowledge.body: Lower quality reduces file size but introduces compression artifacts. 70–80% is a good range for most photographic web images; increase it for images with fine detail or text, decrease it for large galleries where bandwidth matters most.

faq.q: Does this resize my image?
faq.a: Only if you enter a resize width. Otherwise the dimensions are preserved — the workflow only converts to WebP and compresses.

faq.q: Is my image uploaded?
faq.a: No. The optimization runs entirely in your browser. The image never leaves your device.

faq.q: Why is my result larger than the original?
faq.a: If the original was already a tiny, well-compressed WebP, re-encoding may not shrink it further. This is rare; try a lower quality or a resize width.

steps: Browse the table or search for a use, e.g. 'instagram' or 'favicon'.
Filter by category (Social Media, Website, Email, Video Thumbnail, Profile, Print).
Each row shows the recommended width, height, ratio, and formats.
Use the Open Resizer link to open the matching tool and apply the size.
useCases: Finding the right social media post or story dimensions.
Picking an Open Graph image size for link previews.
Choosing a favicon or Apple touch icon size.
Looking up 300 DPI pixel dimensions for photo prints.

knowledge.heading: Recommended, not enforced
knowledge.body: These sizes are commonly recommended values, each with a review date. Platforms and devices change over time, so treat them as starting points and verify against current platform docs for production work.

knowledge.heading: DPI and print sizes
knowledge.body: Print entries show pixel dimensions at 300 DPI, a common minimum for photo printing. A 4×6 inch print at 300 DPI is 1200×1800 pixels. Changing DPI metadata does not add pixels — a smaller image upscaled to these dimensions will not gain detail.

faq.q: Are these the official sizes?
faq.a: They are commonly recommended sizes, each with a review date. Platforms update their guidance, so they are starting points rather than enforced rules.

faq.q: How do I apply a size to my image?
faq.a: Click the Open Resizer link on any row. It opens the matching tool — the Social Media Resizer for social sizes, the Favicon Generator for favicons, the DPI Changer for print sizes, or the Resize tool for the rest.

faq.q: Can I search by ratio?
faq.a: Yes. The search matches names, descriptions, category labels, and ratios — try '1:1' or '16:9'.

steps: Click the upload area and select a HEIC or HEIF photo (iPhone photos are usually .heic).
Choose an output format — JPG for compatibility, PNG for lossless, WebP for the smallest web file.
If you chose JPG or WebP, adjust the quality slider (90% is a good default for photos).
Click Convert. The HEIC is decoded in your browser and re-encoded to your chosen format.
Click Download to save the converted file.
useCases: Opening iPhone HEIC photos on a Windows PC or older software that doesn't read HEIC.
Uploading HEIC photos to a website or form that only accepts JPG or PNG.
Sharing HEIC photos with someone who can't view HEIC.
Reducing file size by converting HEIC to WebP for the web.

knowledge.heading: What HEIC is
knowledge.body: HEIC (High Efficiency Image Container) is the format iPhones use by default since iOS 11. It stores photos at roughly half the size of JPG at the same quality, using the HEVC codec. The trade-off is compatibility: not all browsers, operating systems, and apps can read HEIC, which is why converting to JPG is often necessary.

knowledge.heading: Quality and format choice
knowledge.body: JPG is the safest output for sharing — universally supported. PNG is lossless and supports transparency but produces larger files for photos. WebP gives the smallest files for the web and is supported by all modern browsers. For most iPhone photos, JPG at 90% quality is visually indistinguishable from the original HEIC.

faq.q: Is HEIC better than JPG?
faq.a: HEIC files are about half the size of JPG at similar quality, so they're more efficient. But HEIC is less widely supported — many apps, browsers, and websites can't read it. Converting to JPG makes the photo universally viewable.

faq.q: Does converting HEIC to JPG lose quality?
faq.a: HEIC and JPG are both lossy formats. Converting HEIC to JPG at a high quality setting (90% or above) produces a result that is visually indistinguishable from the original for most photos. At lower quality settings, JPG compression artifacts become visible.

faq.q: Can this tool convert HEIC to PNG or WebP?
faq.a: Yes. Select PNG for a lossless conversion (larger file), or WebP for the smallest web-ready file. JPG is the default because it's the most widely compatible.

faq.q: Are my photos uploaded?
faq.a: No. The HEIC conversion runs entirely in your browser using WebAssembly. Your photos are never uploaded to a server.

about.title: About ImageKitTools
about.metaDescription: About ImageKitTools — a privacy-first, browser-based image toolkit that processes your images locally and keeps cloud storage optional.
paragraphs: ImageKitTools is a privacy-first online image toolkit. Every core tool — compress, resize, convert, crop, rotate, watermark, meme, edit, and blur — runs directly in your browser, so your images are not uploaded to a server by default. You get fast, private results and the file never leaves your device unless you choose to save it.

paragraphs.t: The project is built around four decisions that we will not compromise on: images are processed locally first; core tools require no sign-up; cloud storage is strictly optional and private to you; and the architecture stays a simple modular monolith with browser direct-uploads to private object storage. You can read the details in our

paragraphs: We build one tool at a time and prioritize quality and honesty over breadth. That means real guidance on every tool page — how to use it, when to use it, and what the format and size choices actually mean — instead of thin pages that only exist to rank. Tools report results honestly: if a target file size cannot be reached, we say so rather than silently degrading your image.

ImageKitTools supports eight interface languages and works on desktop and mobile, including touch-based cropping. An optional account lets you save originals and processed results to a private cloud so you can manage them across devices — but the tools themselves never require one.

privacy.title: Privacy Policy
privacy.metaDescription: How ImageKitTools handles your images and data: images are processed in your browser by default, and cloud storage is opt-in and private.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: ImageKitTools is a privacy-first online image toolkit. The core principle is simple: by default, your images are processed entirely inside your browser and are never uploaded to our servers. Cloud features exist, but they are strictly opt-in and only ever act when you explicitly choose to save a file.

sections.heading: Local-first image processing
sections.body: When you use any image tool, the file you select is read by your browser and processed using the browser's Canvas and ImageBitmap APIs. The image bytes do not leave your device. The result you download is generated directly from your browser. There is no server-side copy of images processed with the local tools.

sections.heading: Optional cloud storage
sections.body: If you create an account and choose to save an original or processed image to your cloud, that single file is uploaded directly to private object storage using a short-lived presigned URL. The upload goes straight from your browser to storage; it is not relayed through the application server. Storage keys are generated by the server and never client-controlled. Cloud files are private and accessible only by you, and you can view, download, or delete them at any time from your account. Nothing is uploaded unless you take that explicit action.

sections.heading: Account and authentication
sections.body: To use cloud storage you can register with an email address and password. Passwords are hashed with the Argon2 algorithm before storage; we never store or see your plain password. When you sign in, we set an essential session cookie containing an opaque, random token; only the SHA-256 hash of that token is stored server-side, so a database leak would not expose valid sessions. Email-verification and password-reset tokens are random, single-use, and short-lived (24 hours for verification, 1 hour for resets).

sections.heading: Cookies
sections.body: We use only essential cookies by default: a session cookie (so you stay signed in) and a locale cookie (to remember your language choice). These are necessary for the service to function and are not used for tracking. If analytics are enabled, a measurement cookie may also be set, as described in the Cookie Policy. We do not set advertising cookies.

sections.heading: Analytics and monitoring
sections.body: This site runs third-party analytics (Google Analytics 4) and error monitoring (Sentry) only when the operator has configured them. When enabled, these services may set their own cookies and collect usage data such as page views and errors. No personal image content is ever sent to analytics or monitoring providers. We do not sell or share data with advertisers, and no advertising network is integrated in the current version.

sections.heading: Data retention
sections.body: Cloud files are kept until you delete them. Sessions expire after 30 days of inactivity and are removed when you sign out. Verification and reset tokens expire automatically and are deleted after use. Diagnostic logs, if any, are retained only for the period needed to investigate errors.

sections.heading: Your rights
sections.body: You can review, download, and delete your cloud files at any time from the Cloud files section of your account. You can sign out to end your session immediately. To delete your account and all associated data, contact us using the details on the Contact page.

sections.heading: Security
sections.body: The site is served over HTTPS. Object storage buckets are private with no public read or write access, and all downloads are authorized and issued short-lived URLs. Authentication tokens are hashed at rest. No method of transmission or storage is fully secure, however, and we cannot guarantee absolute security.

sections.heading: Children's privacy
sections.body: ImageKitTools is not directed at children under 13 and we do not knowingly collect personal information from them. If you believe a child has registered an account, please contact us so we can remove it.

sections.heading: Changes to this policy
sections.body: We may update this policy as the service evolves. Changes will be posted on this page with an updated date. Material changes will be highlighted in the app where practical.

sections.heading: Contact
sections.body: Questions about this policy or your data can be sent to the address listed on the Contact page.

You grant us only the limited permission needed to operate the service — to process and, where you instruct, to store and serve your own files back to you.

cookie.title: Cookie Policy
cookie.metaDescription: The cookies used by ImageKitTools: an essential session and locale cookie, with optional analytics only when enabled. No advertising cookies.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: ImageKitTools uses the minimum cookies needed to run the service. By default, only two essential cookies are set. We do not set advertising cookies, and analytics cookies are loaded only if the operator has enabled analytics.

sections.heading: Essential cookies
sections.body: These cookies are required for the site to function and cannot be disabled.

sections.heading: Analytics cookies
sections.body: If Google Analytics 4 is configured by the operator, GA4 may set its own cookies (such as _ga and related identifiers) to measure aggregate usage. These are only present when analytics is enabled, and they collect information like which pages are visited and approximately where visitors come from. They do not collect image content. You can opt out of analytics via your browser settings or a third-party opt-out tool.

sections.heading: No advertising cookies
sections.body: This site does not integrate any advertising network and does not set advertising or cross-site tracking cookies. If advertising is introduced in the future, it will be described here and in the Privacy Policy first.

sections.heading: Managing cookies
sections.body: You can view and delete cookies in your browser settings. Removing the session cookie signs you out; removing the locale cookie resets the interface language to the default. Most browsers also let you block third-party cookies, which will not affect the essential cookies used by this site.
